narrative:
The model estimated a 57.2% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means failure was judged slightly more likely than passing, and the law school used this estimate when it rejected your application.

Three factors drove the decision, in this order. The most influential was your undergraduate GPA, but it worked in your favor: at 3.10 versus an accepted-student average of 3.23, it modestly reduced the predicted risk. The next most influential was your LSAT score, which was the strongest concern against you: at 25, it is well below the accepted average of about 37 and pushed the prediction toward failure. The third factor was your third-year class-rank decile; being in decile 2, compared with an accepted average near 6, also pushed toward failure. Overall, the positive signal from your GPA was outweighed by concerns about your LSAT and third-year standing. Your gender and race were not used.

To improve a future application, address the two main concerns: prepare for and retake the LSAT if feasible, and explain or document any upward trend or context for your third-year rank. Meet with admissions or pre-law advising to build a remediation plan, consider coursework or legal experience that demonstrates readiness, and reapply once you can show stronger evidence. You may also ask whether you can submit a personal statement addressing these factors.
